claim: A rejected paper about a bird's back passage named half your immune system.

start.title: Bird
start.description: Warm-blooded animals with wings and feathers

knots.passage: This material, as well as the output of the intestines, emerges from the bird's cloaca. The cloaca is a multi-purpose opening: waste is expelled through it, most birds mate by joining cloaca, and females lay eggs from it.
knots.hatnote: Birds manage with one all-purpose opening at the back.

knots.passage: The bursa of Fabricius, also known as the cloacal bursa, is a lymphoid organ which aids in the production of B lymphocytes during humoral immunity. The bursa of Fabricius is present during juvenile stages but curls up. For example, the bursa is not visible after sexual maturity in different species of sparrow.
knots.hatnote: Tucked beside it sits a little pouch that young birds can't do without.

knots.passage: It is a specialized organ that, as first demonstrated by Bruce Glick and later by Max Dale Cooper and Robert Good, is necessary for B cell (part of the immune system) development in birds. Mammals generally do not have an equivalent organ; the bone marrow is often the site of both hematopoiesis and B cell development.
knots.hatnote: Its job was cracked by a young poultry scientist, Bruce Glick.

knots.passage: A fellow graduate student, Timothy Chang, worked with Glick's geese in a different study, and noticed that the birds without the Bursa of Fabricius did not produce expected antibodies. Glick and Chang wrote up the results of this study and were unable to get it published in Science, so it was published in Poultry Science in 1956. Their publication, considered a landmark paper, is one of the most cited works from Poultry Science.
knots.hatnote: The discovery was an accident, and the top journal turned it down.

knots.passage: Scientists building on Glick's work combined bursectomy with thymectomy to demonstrate that the bursa controlled immune responses associated with circulating antibodies, whereas the thymus controlled cellular immunity. Chicken research was the first source of the two-component (B cells and T cells concept) of immunity.
knots.hatnote: That humble paper split immunity in two.

knots.passage: In mammals, B cells mature in the bone marrow, which is at the core of most bones. In birds, B cells mature in the bursa of Fabricius, a lymphoid organ where they were first discovered by Timothy Chang and Bruce Glick, which is why the B stands for bursa and not bone marrow, as commonly believed.
knots.hatnote: And it left its mark on the name.

payoff: Every B cell in your body is named after a pouch in a bird's rear, found by accident and first rejected by Science.
